record.content_text:
In Chapter 3 you learnt about the base two number system. The base two or binary number system counts in groups of 2, and uses only the digits 0 and 1 to represent any number. The numbers in the base two number system are called binary numbers.

We can use place value tables in the base two number system. The place values are powers of 2. For example:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
    \hline
    \text{thirty twos} & \text{sixteens} & \text{eights} & \text{fours} & \text{twos} & \text{units} \\
    (2^5) & (2^4) & (2^3) & (2^2) & (2^1) & (2^0) \\
    \hline
    &  &  & & & \\
    \hline
    \end{array}
$$

The binary numbers that correspond to the decimal numbers 1 to 10 are:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|}
    \hline
    \text{decimal number} & \text{binary number} \\
    \hline
    1& 1 \\
    2& 10 \\
    3& 11 \\
    4& 100 \\
    5& 101 \\
    6& 110 \\
    7& 111 \\
    8& 1000 \\
    9& 1001 \\
    10& 1010 \\
    \hline
    \end{array}
$$

We use subscripts to tell us which system a certain combination of digits belong to. For example:
- $100_{10}$ or $100_{\text{ten}}$ means one hundred
- $100_2$ or $100_{\text{two}}$ means four

In this chapter you will learn how to add, subtract and multiply binary numbers.

record_links.rationale: This worked example converts a decimal number to a binary number by repeated division by 2.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 3.3: Converting decimal numbers to binary numbers

record.evidence_quote: Write $23_\text{ten}$ as a base two number.
record.prompt_text:
Write
 $23_\text{ten}$ as a base two number.
record.answer_text:
- 
 Step 1: Divide the given number repeatedly by 2, until you get zero. For each division, write down whether
 the remainder is 0 or 1.

 
 $$
\begin{array}{r|rr}
 2 & 23 & \\
 \hline
 2 & 11 & \text{remainder: }1 \\
 \hline
 2 & 5 & \text{remainder: }1 \\
 \hline
 2 & 2 & \text{remainder: }1 \\
 \hline
 2 & 1 & \text{remainder: }0 \\
 \hline
 & 0 & \text{remainder: }1 \\
 \hline
 \end{array}
$$ 

 - 
 Step 2: Write down the remainders from bottom to top. This gives the corresponding binary number.

 $$
10111
$$
 $$
\therefore 23_\text{ten}= 10111_\text{two}
$$

closest_candidate_atomic_objectives.proposed_objective_text: Write decimal numbers as sums of powers of 2.
closest_candidate_atomic_objectives.evidence_quote: To work with binary numbers, you need to be able to write a decimal number as the sum of powers of 2.
closest_candidate_atomic_objectives.rationale: The textbook explicitly teaches and assesses decomposing decimal numbers into powers of 2 before full binary conversion. That prerequisite is measurable, but it is not equivalent to converting a base 10 numeral into a binary number.

closest_candidate_atomic_objectives.proposed_objective_text: Convert binary numbers to base ten numbers.
closest_candidate_atomic_objectives.evidence_quote: Convert binary numbers to base ten numbers
closest_candidate_atomic_objectives.rationale: The textbook includes a worked example and exercises for binary-to-base-ten conversion. This is the reverse direction of the canonical AO and should be reviewed as a possible missing adjacent objective rather than silently linked to the base-ten-to-binary AO.
